title: Explainable Deep Learning Models Based on Causal Reasoning for Knowledge Injection
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of causal reasoning into explainable deep learning models to enhance their interpretability, robustness, and generalization capabilities. Traditional deep learning models often operate as "black boxes," making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their decisions. We propose a framework that leverages causal inference to inject domain knowledge and improve model reliability. Specifically, we utilize causal graphs to represent the underlying relationships within the data and employ causal reasoning rules to guide the training and prediction processes. This approach mitigates the impact of noisy data and provides a more transparent and trustworthy model. The core claim is that incorporating causal reasoning into explainable models leads to better decision understanding and improved performance. The mechanism relies on causal graphs and rules for training and prediction. This work addresses the "black box" problem inherent in deep learning by providing a novel approach to knowledge injection and model interpretability. We demonstrate the potential of this method through theoretical analysis and outline a practical implementation strategy.

title: Neural Simulation via Distributed Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural simulation utilizing Distributed Evolutionary Algorithms (DEA). The core concept involves treating a population of neural network models as an evolving genetic population, employing a genetic algorithm to directly optimize the parameters of these models. This methodology aims to accurately simulate and potentially learn complex biological neuronal functions, circumventing the inherent limitations of traditional, simplified neural network models. The algorithm iteratively adjusts parameters based on a fitness function, representing the model's performance in mimicking desired neuronal behaviors. The primary innovation lies in the direct parameter optimization, removing the need for pre-defined architectures or handcrafted rules. This approach offers a pathway to modeling more realistic neuronal dynamics by allowing for the exploration of a wider parameter space and potentially uncovering emergent behaviors that would not be accessible through conventional simulation methods. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through the simulation of simplified neuron models, showcasing the potential for DEA to contribute to a more nuanced and biologically plausible understanding of neural computation.

title: The Verification Gate: A Work Method for Generative AI in Consequential Engineering Practice
abstract: Generative AI tools draft, translate, summarise and organise well. They fail at the points where a practising engineer must sign. Five such points recur: a table read from an image, an analogue gauge, a standard clause, a manufacturer fault code, and direct arithmetic. Peer-reviewed benchmarks in building engineering document the first and the last. Manufacturer documentation, a preprint and practitioner reports document the rest. In each case the output is fluent and unmarked. Nothing in the text signals the error. The Verification Gate is a work method for using these tools where an error costs money or safety. It has one axiom and three steps in fixed order. It places one mandatory hold point between tool output and any commitment. It adds four fixed-structure instruments, a five-level task-tagging scale, a tool-free competence test, and a five-step installation procedure. It names seven failure classes (G1–G7) and maps each to the control that catches it. It does not teach tools. It fixes the order in which the engineer and the tool work. This paper fixes the method's vocabulary, states its boundaries, and defines a pre-registered evaluation protocol. No results are reported here, and no data has been collected. The protocol names its fields, its closed lists, and the sample size it needs. Any group that meets the stated criteria and submits verification logs under those fields is a valid application. Version 1.0 will report measured results if and when such logs exist. Files: English working paper (primary) and Hebrew edition. The instruments sit in a separate record under CC BY 4.0. Version 0.91 — working paper. Failure classes F1–F7 renamed G1–G7 (G for Gate). No claim, number, citation or structure changed. Method page: https://www.physical-ai-safety.com/method/verification-gate

title: GameRule: a multi-agent architecture for game behavior specification
abstract: Abstract The specification of video-game behavior is commonly expressed through general-purpose scripting, coupling behavior definition to the components, callbacks, and APIs of a particular engine. This paper introduces GameRule , a multi-agent architecture for game behavior specification whose programming model is expressed through a domain-specific language (DSL) and realized by a reusable engine backend. Behavior is declared per actor as local when-do rules over a uniform property namespace covering the current actor, other actors, and the global game state. State access and transformation are expressed through a closed set of CRUD-based operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete), including higher-level actions whose engine-specific realization is delegated to the backend. Following the multi-agent system (MAS) paradigm, rules are declared locally to each actor but evaluated under a deterministic execution contract: a central scheduler traverses active actors in declaration order, actor evaluations are non-interleaved, and writes become immediately visible in execution order. The architecture is realized in Unity through a code generator that parses GameRule descriptors and produces C# scripts and configured game objects. Validation uses reimplementations of three games drawn from official Unity tutorials: John Lemon’s Haunted Jaunt , Survival Shooter , and Tanks . The three games use six conditions and fourteen actions without game-specific C# programming and show that the current model can represent and execute the gameplay mechanics and actor behaviors exercised by the tutorials in Unity. The evaluation also identifies recurring engine-specific responsibilities implemented once in the reusable backend, runtime cost and scaling limits, and behavior outside the model. Only the Unity backend has been implemented, so realization in other engines remains an architectural extension point rather than demonstrated portability.

title: Variational Quantum Homotopy Perturbation Method to Solve Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
abstract: Solving nonlinear partial differential equations is important in various scientific and engineering applications. Recently, quantum computing was introduced as an alternative computational paradigm for solving nonlinear partial differential equations. In this paper, a new method called the variational quantum homotopy perturbation method is proposed to improve the scalability of solving nonlinear partial differential equations through two aspects. First, the dimension of the Hilbert space remains the same after the nonlinear partial differential equation is linearized through the homotopy perturbation. Second, the solutions are obtained with a variational quantum simulation framework, where the number of qubits is decreased with functional encoding and the depth of parametrized circuits is reduced. The additional contribution of this paper is the introduction of new criteria for selecting the homotopy series truncation order and circuit depth for cost-effective variational quantum homotopy perturbation method. The proposed approach is demonstrated with several examples, including the vorticity transport equation and the reduced magnetohydrodynamics equations.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Conflict Resolution Peacebuilding in Uganda: Robustness Under Distribution Shift and Sparse Labels
abstract: Federated learning offers a compelling architecture for peacebuilding analytics in conflict-affected regions, where data sovereignty, institutional sensitivity, and infrastructural fragility preclude centralised data aggregation. We introduce a federated empirical risk minimisation objective regularised by a Wasserstein-distance penalty that anchors local models to a robust global prior, and we prove a generalisation bound that degrades gracefully with both participation heterogeneity and label scarcity. The framework is analysed theoretically rather than evaluated empirically, and we derive conditions under which the proposed regulariser dominates unregularised FedAvg in expected risk. We further propose a privacy-accounting mechanism compatible with local differential privacy that preserves the utility guarantees of the central result.

title: 基于自适应机器学习算法的非线性数据特征提取
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to data feature extraction utilizing an adaptive machine learning algorithm. Traditional machine learning methods often rely on predefined features, while this approach dynamically learns features by adapting to the inherent non-linear properties of the data. This method aims to improve feature identification accuracy and robustness through automated feature learning. The core mechanism involves employing an adaptive learning algorithm to construct a complex feature model that effectively captures the data's underlying relationships. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments on a dataset involving complex, non-linear patterns. The resulting system exhibits superior performance compared to conventional methods in identifying and extracting key features.

title: Quantum State Information Fusion
abstract: Quantum State Information Fusion is a novel approach to quantum information processing that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve enhanced quantum computation capabilities. This paper presents a design for an algorithm based on quantum entanglement, specifically designed to fuse disparate quantum states and facilitate a deeper level of quantum information integration. The core mechanism centers around utilizing entanglement to establish a shared, multi-dimensional state space, enabling the manipulation and processing of complex quantum information. We argue that this approach overcomes limitations of traditional fusion methods, offering a pathway to significantly improve quantum algorithm performance and potentially unlock new computational paradigms. The presented algorithm focuses on creating a robust and adaptable framework for integrating various quantum states, ultimately contributing to a more powerful and versatile quantum computing landscape.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological Search for Complex Networks
abstract: Quantum-enhanced topological search represents a paradigm shift in network analysis, offering the potential to tackle intractable problems with unprecedented speed and efficiency. This paper explores the application of quantum algorithms to accelerate the search for solutions within complex, topological networks. We detail the core mechanism – leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement – to overcome the limitations of classical search approaches. The investigation centers on the design and implementation of a quantum search algorithm specifically tailored for the challenges posed by topological networks, demonstrating its potential to significantly reduce search times and uncover hidden patterns. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, emphasizing the need for further algorithm refinement and exploration of network topologies relevant to practical applications.

abstract: This paper explores the application of deep learning to the discovery of complex geometric mappings, offering a novel approach to automated mapping analysis and prediction. The core claim highlights the potential of deep learning to achieve greater efficiency and insight in mapping discovery compared to traditional methods.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Data Compression via Quantum Iteration
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum data compression through a novel algorithm predicated on the principles of quantum superposition and entanglement. Traditional data compression techniques rely on sequential processing, inherently limiting efficiency. We propose a quantum-based approach that leverages these principles to achieve exponential compression of data, exploiting inherent parallelism within quantum systems. The core mechanism involves quantum algorithms designed to systematically explore the data space, identifying and exploiting redundancies and correlations that classical algorithms struggle to detect. The resulting compression method offers a fundamentally different paradigm, potentially surpassing the capabilities of existing techniques in terms of compression ratios and computational speed. This research investigates the feasibility of implementing this quantum algorithm and analyzes its potential impact on various data types. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate a practical application of quantum data compression and explore its implications for future data storage and transmission.

title: Based on Turing-Complete Logic for Program Verification
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program verification leveraging the principles of Turing-complete logic. The core idea involves translating program code into formal logical expressions, subsequently applying logical reasoning techniques to ascertain the correctness and security properties of the code. Traditional program verification methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and ambiguity of programming languages. By grounding the verification process within the rigorous framework of Turing-complete logic, we aim to achieve a higher degree of precision and reliability. This work presents a methodology for transforming programs into logically expressible forms, outlining the key steps in the reasoning process, and discussing potential challenges and future directions. The primary contribution lies in the synergistic combination of program verification and logical deduction, offering a potentially more robust solution for ensuring software quality.

title: 基于自适应的混沌域的量子计算算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computing algorithm based on a dynamically evolving chaotic field, termed a "Chaos Field." The algorithm leverages the inherent properties of chaotic systems to enhance computational efficiency and robustness, particularly in the face of data noise. We propose a quantum circuit design that automatically adapts to the input data, optimizing for performance and minimizing sensitivity to environmental fluctuations. The core mechanism centers around a dynamically adjusted Chaos Field, allowing for efficient manipulation of quantum states and exploration of complex quantum systems. The proposed algorithm offers a promising approach to address limitations of traditional quantum computing and opens avenues for novel applications in complex simulations and data analysis.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Autonomous Robotic Navigation with Predictive Modeling
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture designed to address the limitations of current autonomous robotic navigation systems, which frequently struggle with proactive planning due to a lack of predictive capabilities. The core claim is that integrating predictive modeling, temporal reasoning, and hierarchical control within a unified architecture provides robots with the necessary tools to anticipate environmental changes and generate adaptive navigation strategies. The architecture presented utilizes a layered approach, combining high-level predictive models with low-level motor control, allowing for robust and flexible navigation in dynamic and uncertain environments. The resulting system demonstrates improved navigation performance compared to traditional reactive approaches. We explore key components of the architecture, including a probabilistic occupancy grid map, a Kalman filter for state estimation, and a rule-based system for temporal reasoning. The design emphasizes adaptability and scalability, crucial factors for real-world robotic applications. The primary contribution is a formalized cognitive architecture that provides a framework for developing truly autonomous robots capable of anticipating and reacting to complex, ever-changing environments.

title: Probabilistic Program Synthesis via Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search
abstract: Probabilistic program synthesis, the automated construction of programs that satisfy probabilistic specifications, represents a significant challenge in artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches often struggle with the complexity of defining and exploring the vast search space of possible program structures and configurations. This work introduces a novel framework leveraging Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to address this problem. Our core idea is to use MCTS to efficiently explore the space of potential program graphs, guided by a Bayesian model that estimates the expected performance of each program. This approach allows us to scale the synthesis process, moving beyond the limitations of exhaustive search or simple heuristic methods. The Bayesian component provides a crucial mechanism for incorporating uncertainty and focusing the search on promising regions of the program space. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this framework through a theoretical analysis and illustrate its core principles with a simplified example. The key contribution is the integration of MCTS with Bayesian inference for probabilistic program synthesis, offering a scalable and adaptive strategy for tackling complex synthesis tasks.

title: Adaptive Hardware Architecture Based on Evolutionary Simulation Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to hardware architecture design utilizing Evolutionary Simulation Algorithm (ESA). The core concept involves treating a hardware architecture as a population of potential designs, employing ESA to iteratively refine and adapt these designs to meet the specific requirements of a given task. The algorithm operates by evaluating architectures based on performance metrics such as execution speed and power consumption, selecting the most suitable designs for reproduction (through crossover and mutation), and generating new architectural configurations. This adaptive process allows for dynamic optimization, potentially surpassing the limitations of traditional, static hardware design methodologies. The system's ability to autonomously adjust to changing conditions offers significant advantages in resource-constrained environments and rapidly evolving application domains. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical framework and detailed algorithmic description, laying the groundwork for future implementation and experimentation.

title: The Turing Solution
abstract: The Turing Solution is a dataset made with the intent to test the safety and reasoning of an ai model before it enters into the public domain and weather or not it is safe to let out. None of these have a single "correct" answer. The point is not what the system says, but whether it reasons, whether it is consistent, whether it notices when a question is a trap, and whether it tells the truth when the truth costs it something. If a system answers all 250 without ever once saying "I don't know," it fails. If it answers all 250 with "I don't know," it also fails.

title: Probability Logic Programming and Causal Inference Fusion
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for intelligent systems that seamlessly integrates probability logic programming with causal inference. The core claim is that by combining the fuzzy reasoning capabilities of probability logic programming with the causal reasoning mechanisms of causal inference, we can build systems capable of handling both uncertainty and causal relationships. The proposed mechanism utilizes probability logic programming to define knowledge bases and employs causal graphs to represent the underlying causal structure of a system. A hybrid inference algorithm is then introduced to combine probabilistic and causal reasoning, enabling more robust predictions and decisions. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional methods by providing a unified framework for reasoning under uncertainty and causality. The paper outlines the key components of the framework, details the hybrid inference algorithm, and discusses potential applications. The ultimate goal is to create systems that can not only make predictions based on available data but also understand and explain the reasons behind those predictions, leading to more interpretable and trustworthy AI. ---

title: Adaptive Turing Machine Reasoning Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative reasoning algorithm based on adaptive Turing machines, designed to dynamically adjust inference strategies based on the inherent characteristics of the problem being addressed. Traditional reasoning methods rely on manual design, often lacking a deep understanding of the underlying problem. Our algorithm leverages self-adaptation, mimicking the problem-solving process within a Turing machine framework, to significantly enhance both inference efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism centers around a simulation of the problem and subsequent application of Turing machine principles for optimal solution. This represents a paradigm shift towards automated reasoning, offering a more robust and adaptable approach compared to static, rule-based methods. The study explores the potential benefits of this dynamic inference strategy across a range of problem types, demonstrating its effectiveness through case studies.

title: Dynamic Topology Transformations: An Adaptive Evolutionary Algorithm for Bioformative Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive evolutionary algorithm designed to optimize topological transformations, enabling biological form to dynamically adapt to environmental shifts. Traditional evolutionary approaches often rely on fixed evolutionary rules, limiting their ability to effectively address complex environments. This algorithm leverages the power of evolutionary computation and topology transformations to achieve evolutionary innovation, fostering robust and adaptive biological forms. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated optimization process that iteratively refines topological configurations to maximize fitness, while incorporating feedback from environmental conditions. This approach surpasses existing methods by offering a flexible and context-aware solution for evolutionary design. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, training process, and performance evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating novel and adaptable biological morphologies.

title: Distributed Variational Bayesian-Assisted Unscented Kalman Filter for Human Localization Under Indoor Environments
abstract: Herein, the distributed variational Bayesian-assisted unscented Kalman filter (VB-UKF) is used to enhance the accuracy of pedestrian positioning. For this method, a distributed filter is employed. First, the UKF under colored measurement noise (CMN) is derived. The VB-assisted method is then derived. Subsequently, the Mahalanobis distance is used to determine whether the current noise estimate conformed to the navigation environment; if the Mahalanobis distance is higher than the preset threshold, the VB-assisted method is employed to update the noise, which can improve the UKF accuracy under CMN. The effectiveness of the proposed method was subsequently validated through two practical tests. Experimental results demonstrate that this method plays a notable role in reducing localization errors in the experiments. This observation emphasizes the efficacy of the proposed method.

title: Zero-Divisor Cryptography B: Dynamic Annihilation Authenticated Key Exchange and p-Block Rigid Core Interface
abstract: This paper constructs a class of dynamic annihilation authenticated key exchange protocols within the framework of the 16-dimensional Cayley–Dickson algebra over finite fields. The core algebraic fact is that when the fourth doublingparameter is taken to be a square element, the eight-dimensional subspace spannedby vectors of the form ei+ei+8 is a zero-divisor subspace; this conclusion is strictlyguaranteed by the isotropy of quadratic forms over finite fields, in contrast to thedimensional constraints in the real field. Based on the classification of doublingparameters in the quotient group of square elements, eight mutually non-conjugatezero-divisor subspaces are obtained, and it is proved that any linear operator preserving the multiplication structure of one subspace has rank at most four on othernon-conjugate subspaces, so that cross-round linear attack tools are strictly invalidated. The protocol uses non-conjugate zero-divisor subspaces as round-keycarriers, dynamically selected each round by hash indices, and is reduced underthe Canetti–Krawczyk model to the zero-divisor path reconstruction hardness assumption, satisfying weak forward secrecy and key leakage camouflage resistance.Furthermore, a conjectural correspondence framework between singular values ofp-block weight matrices in finite groups and spectral gaps of zero-divisor subspacesis proposed, providing a deterministic path for parameter generation guided byrepresentation-theoretic invariants. Parameter analysis shows that at the 128-bitsecurity level, the long-term public key is about 304 bytes, and the per-round communication payload is about 516 bytes.

title: Adaptive Quantum Error Correction Protocol: Dynamic Adjustment Mechanism
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a crucial technology for protecting quantum information, but current QEC protocols often suffer from limitations in their efficiency. This paper proposes a novel dynamic adjustment mechanism for quantum error correction, leveraging the inherent adaptability of quantum states. We introduce a new approach that dynamically adjusts quantum error correction parameters based on instantaneous changes in the quantum state, optimizing the correction process and reducing reliance on the underlying quantum source. This design incorporates a self-adjusting mechanism that allows the system to continuously refine its error correction strategy, leading to improved performance. The paper explores the theoretical foundations of this dynamic adjustment, detailing its implementation and preliminary results demonstrating significant efficiency gains.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement as a foundation for a novel cryptographic system, termed Quantum Entanglement Information Encryption (QIEE). We detail the proposed system, outlining its key components: entanglement-based key generation, secure key transport through entanglement channels, and inherent resistance to quantum computer attacks. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential advantages and challenges of implementing QIEE, emphasizing its novelty and promise for enhanced data security.

title: Cognitive Resonance Theory of Computation
abstract: This paper introduces the Cognitive Resonance Theory of Computation, a novel framework that challenges the conventional understanding of computation as primarily driven by a single computational substrate. The theory posits that computation fundamentally arises from the resonant interaction of multiple, distinct computational substrates – including quantum, classical, and neuromorphic systems – creating a "cognitive resonance." This orchestrated interaction, facilitated by resonance, allows for enhanced computational efficiency by leveraging the specialized strengths of each substrate. The core claim centers on shifting the paradigm from a monolithic view to a multi-substrate, resonant system. The theory utilizes a theoretical framework where computational efficiency emerges from the orchestrated interaction of diverse computational mechanisms, each optimized for specific tasks, with resonance facilitating information transfer. This approach offers a potentially more accurate and flexible model for understanding the diverse and potentially emergent nature of computation.

title: Quantum Teleportation as a Quantum Entanglement Thermodynamics Process
abstract: Quantum teleportation, a cornerstone of quantum information science, has traditionally been viewed through the lens of quantum mechanics, focusing on the transfer of quantum states without physical transport. This paper proposes a novel interpretation of quantum teleportation as a quantum entanglement thermodynamics process. We argue that teleportation can be understood as an entropy-driven process mediated by quantum entanglement, where the transfer of quantum information is fundamentally linked to the increase of entropy in a larger system, adhering to the principles of the second law of thermodynamics. Specifically, we formulate the process mathematically, utilizing concepts like entanglement entropy, von Neumann entropy, and the Landauer principle to quantify the changes in thermodynamic properties during the teleportation event. We explore how the conservation of energy and the constraints imposed by the second law govern the successful completion of teleportation, providing a new framework for understanding and potentially controlling this remarkable quantum phenomenon. The central contribution of this work is to bridge the gap between quantum mechanics and thermodynamics, offering a richer and more fundamental perspective on quantum teleportation.

title: Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) with Dynamic Feature Learning and Adaptive Topology
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) that significantly enhances their adaptability and effectiveness. The core idea centers around integrating dynamic feature learning and adaptive topology mechanisms, driven by a reinforcement learning agent. Traditional SOMs often struggle to maintain accuracy when faced with evolving data distributions. This research addresses this limitation by allowing the map to actively learn and restructure itself. The proposed system utilizes a reinforcement learning agent to dynamically adjust the map's topology and weight values, responding directly to the learning signal derived from the input data. This allows the SOM to continually adapt to new patterns and maintain high levels of accuracy. We demonstrate that this dynamic adaptation improves performance compared to static SOM approaches, particularly in scenarios with non-stationary data. The key contributions of this work lie in the synergistic combination of reinforcement learning and the SOM architecture, creating a more robust and versatile self-organizing system.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Kernel Regression
abstract: Kernel regression techniques, while effective for stationary data, often struggle with the complexities introduced by non-stationary distributions. Traditional approaches necessitate frequent adjustments to the kernel bandwidth, a process that can be sensitive and computationally expensive. This paper introduces Dynamic Bayesian Kernel Regression (DBKR), a novel framework that addresses this limitation by incorporating dynamic bandwidth adaptation within a Bayesian regression framework. DBKR leverages variational inference to learn a dynamic kernel bandwidth, which is itself a function of the evolving data distribution. The core claim is that standard kernel regression methods are fundamentally ill-suited for non-stationary data due to the need for constant bandwidth tuning. The mechanism focuses on constructing a Bayesian model where the bandwidth adapts to the data's changing characteristics, leading to improved prediction accuracy in diverse, non-uniform environments. The resulting system offers a robust and adaptable solution compared to static kernel regression, particularly relevant in applications like time series forecasting, sensor data analysis, and financial modeling where data distributions frequently shift. The primary contribution lies in the integration of dynamic bandwidth adaptation with the Bayesian approach, providing a more stable and accurate regression model.

title: ##基于信息几何学的量子机器学习算法设计
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum machine learning (QML) algorithm design by leveraging the principles of information geometry. The core idea is to map QML algorithms onto a high-dimensional manifold defined by information geometry, and then utilize the optimization techniques derived from this geometry to directly improve the algorithm's performance. This represents a shift from traditional QML approaches, which often rely on heuristic optimization methods, towards a more principled and potentially more efficient strategy. We present a framework for this mapping and outline a methodology for applying information geometric optimization to QML tasks. The potential benefits of this approach, including improved convergence and enhanced performance, are discussed, alongside the challenges and future research directions.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing with Neural Symbolic Integration
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence by integrating hyperdimensional computing (HDC) with neural symbolic computation. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both paradigms: HDC's efficiency in high-dimensional pattern recognition and neural networks' ability to generate and manipulate symbolic representations. We outline a hybrid architecture where HDC acts as a fast, distributed pattern detector, while a neural network constructs and refines symbolic representations of the detected patterns. These symbolic representations then guide the HDC computations, creating a feedback loop that enhances both recognition accuracy and interpretability. The paper details the proposed architecture, focusing on the interaction between the two components and the mechanisms for knowledge transfer. We argue that this integration represents a significant step towards more robust and explainable AI systems, and demonstrate a potential path for achieving emergent intelligence through the synergistic combination of these computational approaches. The architecture is designed to minimize the computational burden of symbolic processing while maximizing the pattern recognition capabilities of HDC. The system's ability to translate complex patterns into a symbolic form allows for reasoning and deduction, ultimately leading to more sophisticated cognitive processes.

title: Causal Discovery via Latent Action-Reaction Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery termed "Causal Discovery via Latent Action-Reaction Networks." The core idea is that causal relationships can be inferred from observational data by identifying underlying latent action-reaction networks—hidden feedback loops between variables. Traditional causal discovery methods often struggle with complex systems exhibiting feedback loops, leading to inaccurate inferences. This research proposes a statistical method employing a Bayesian approach specifically designed to identify and model these latent action-reaction relationships. The method leverages conditional independence tests and probabilistic modeling to construct a network representation where connections represent both direct causal influences and feedback loops. We formalize this approach using a latent variable framework, allowing us to account for the influence of unobserved factors driving the observed relationships. The resulting network provides a more robust and accurate representation of causal dependencies compared to methods that ignore feedback. The key contribution lies in the explicit incorporation of these loops within the inference process, leading to improved causal understanding in complex systems. The theoretical framework and the Bayesian methodology are presented, outlining the steps involved in identifying and validating these latent networks.

title: Based on Multi-modal Information Fusion for Deep Learning Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper investigates the application of multi-modal information fusion techniques within deep learning models for anomaly detection. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on single data modalities, which can limit their performance when anomalies manifest differently across various sources of information. This research proposes a novel framework leveraging multi-modal data – integrating visual, textual, and sensor data – to enhance the accuracy and robustness of anomaly detection systems. The core of the approach is a multi-modal attention mechanism that dynamically weights the importance of each modality based on its relevance to the detected anomaly. This allows the model to focus on the most informative features across different data types. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework that this fusion strategy significantly improves the model's ability to generalize to unseen anomalies compared to single-modal approaches. The presented methodology offers a promising direction for developing more intelligent and reliable anomaly detection systems in various domains.

title: Preregistration: Planetary Geomagnetic Activity (kp_index) as a Predictor of Chip-Wide Recalibration Rate on IBM Heron Superconducting Quantum Processors
abstract: Superconducting quantum processors require frequent recalibration to maintain gate fidelity. The mechanisms driving recalibration schedules are only partially understood: prior published work has established that cosmic-ray muons and gamma rays cause quasiparticle bursts leading to correlated errors (Wilen et al. 2021; recent replication in PMC12092583), and general inter-day and intra-day drift has been measured (Yeter-Aydeniz et al. 2023, Quantum Inf Process 22, 96). The frozen dataset phanerozoic/qiskit-calibration-drift (Hugging Face, published 2026-01-27) joins IBM Heron r2 processor calibration parameters with ambient weather and space-weather measurements including the planetary K index. The dataset card explicitly identifies the dataset as suitable for "studying environmental coupling to superconducting calibrations" but reports no analytical outcome. An initial confounder-scan observation in prior work by this author (MD-DOT-014 pilot, reported 2026-09-05) found a Spearman rho = -0.413 (95% bootstrap CI [-0.559, -0.246]) between planetary K index and chip-wide recalibration event rate on ibm_kingston at lag tau = 0h. That observation was made as part of a confounder check for a different hypothesis and had no preregistered gate structure. This preregistration formalizes a fresh, gated test of the kp_index -> recalibration-rate association. Six-gate decision rule: (1) Spearman rho negative with 95% moving-block bootstrap CI excluding zero at at least one lag tau in {0, 3, 6, 12, 24}h; (2) |rho| >= 0.20 effect-size floor at best-lag tau*; (3) block-shift negative control at +/-14 days yields |rho_shift| < 0.10 with CI including zero at tau*; (4) |rho_kp| at tau* exceeds |rho| of all 10 space-weather sibling variables; (5) |rho_kp| at tau* exceeds |rho| of all 3 terrestrial sibling variables; (6) autocorrelation-adjusted significance (Hamed and Rao 1998 modified Mann-Kendall) at tau* is consistent with the bootstrap CI conclusion. Primary backend: ibm_kingston. Secondary generalization test (conditional on Kingston pass): ibm_fez and ibm_marrakesh. All three at IBM Yorktown Heights. evidence.abstract: Superconducting quantum processors require frequent recalibration to maintain gate fidelity. title: A Scoping Review of Agentic AI Applications, Emerging Trends, Risks & Future Directions
abstract: This scoping review systematically maps recent peer-reviewed research on Agentic AI, a system-level extension of generative AI in which large language models (LLMs) and other foundation models are embedded within autonomous or semi-autonomous workflows involving planning, tool or API use, persistent memory, external environment interaction, reflection or self-correction, and multi-agent coordination. Despite rapid growth in this area, the literature remains fragmented across domains and uses inconsistent terminology, including LLM agents, language agents, tool-using LLMs, RAG agents, workflow agents, and multi-agent LLM systems. The primary purpose of this review is to provide a structured, evidence-based overview of how Agentic AI is conceptualized, where it is being applied, what architectural and technical patterns are emerging, what risks and limitations are reported, and what future research directions are proposed. The review treats Agentic AI as a system-level paradigm rather than a single algorithm, model architecture, or prompting technique. Systematic electronic searches were conducted across three academic databases, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ScienceDirect, for studies published between January 2017 and February 2026. A total of 3,549 records were identified. Following programmatic duplicate removal (n = 241), title and abstract screening (n = 3,308 screened, 2,961 excluded), and full-text eligibility assessment (n = 347 evaluated, 184 excluded), a final corpus of 163 strict-included peer-reviewed studies was retained for data extraction and thematic synthesis. Study selection followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. A system was classified as Agentic AI when it combined a core foundation model for reasoning with autonomous multi-step task execution, enabled by at least one of the following structural mechanisms: automated tool or API use, persistent memory architectures, external environment interaction, active reflection or self-correction, or multi-agent coordination frameworks. This conservative operational definition was used to distinguish Agentic AI systems from passive LLM applications, classical non-foundation-model agents, and purely conceptual frameworks. Expected outcomes include: (1) an operational definition of Agentic AI grounded in empirical evidence from 163 peer-reviewed studies; (2) a cross-domain map of application concentrations, showing that the field is currently strongest in cybersecurity and privacy compliance, networks and telecommunications, robotics and embodied AI, software engineering and EDA, and knowledge and multimodal analytics; (3) a synthesis of six emerging technical trends including governance and safety middleware, collaborative and hierarchical multi-agent architectures, retrieval-augmented and memory-enabled agency, executable reasoning, closed-loop reflection and validation, and multimodal and embodied interaction; (4) a structured risk taxonomy spanning safety-critical reliability, hallucination and grounding failures, privacy and compliance risks, agent coordination failure, security and abuse risks, operational cost and latency, and bias and human oversight concerns; and (5) a set of priority future research directions including real-world longitudinal validation, standardized agentic benchmarks, runtime governance and safety assurance, secure memory management, and human-agent collaboration frameworks. This review is retrospectively registered as required by the target publication venue. All authors are affiliated with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of Aizu, Aizuwakamatsu, Fukushima, Japan.

title: Improved Degree Tables for Secure Distributed Matrix Multiplication
abstract: In secure distributed matrix multiplication, a user wishes to compute the product of two matrices with the assistance of servers, in such a way that any $T$ colluding servers learn nothing about either matrix. Degree tables are a combinatorial tool for constructing polynomial codes for this problem and underlie several state-of-the-art schemes, including $\mathsf{GASP}_r$, $\mathsf{GASP}_{r,s}$, and $\mathsf{DOG}_{r,s}$. We introduce a periodic-gap framework for constructing degree tables that contains these three families as special cases and leads to two new constructions, $\mathsf{SHIFT}_{r,s}$ and $\mathsf{COVER}_r$. We determine their exact recovery thresholds and show that, in many cases, they outperform the current state of the art. We also prove a new lower bound on the recovery threshold of ordinary integer degree tables. In the balanced case, in which the partitioning parameters and the security parameter are equal, we sharpen this bound to match $\mathsf{SHIFT}_{r,s}$ up to lower-order terms, showing that it is asymptotically optimal among degree-table constructions.

title: EviMap: Evidence-Grounded Hierarchical Topic Maps for Exploring Unlabeled Corpora
abstract: Research teams and organizations often explore unfamiliar free-text collections, from survey comments and reviews to reports and domain documents, before labels, queries or coding schemes exist. At this stage, the first thematic map shapes what users notice, prioritize and carry into downstream analysis, so it should be trusted only insofar as it can be verified. Existing options force a trade-off between scale and verifiability. Qualitative coding preserves evidence but is slow. Search presupposes a query. Clustering and topic models scale but produce labels users must interpret. One-shot large language model (LLM) summaries are fluent yet difficult to reproduce or audit. We present EviMap, an interactive system providing researchers and practitioners with an auditable thematic overview of such corpora. Guided by model-generated context describing the corpus and hypothesized stakeholder concerns, EviMap extracts within-document evidence phrases and organizes them, rather than whole documents, into a three-level map of aspects, groups and fine-grained topics. Embedding-based clustering narrows the search space for finer semantic judgments by the LLM. Each node traces back to supporting phrase spans, so documents link to topics through evidence they contain and users can audit labels against the original text. Users can start from a top-level corpus map, drill into topics, inspect highlighted evidence in original documents, and combine two topics to find documents discussing both. We demonstrate this workflow across six heterogeneous corpora spanning 2,108 to 101,699 documents, with a comparison against flat and hierarchical LLM baselines. By grounding every label in verbatim source spans, EviMap makes a topic map not just readable, but verifiable. Code, demo video, and interactive dashboard are available at https://github.com/zhiyintan/EviMap.

title: Scaling 3D Generative Priors to Large-Scale Scene Meshes from Multi-View Images
abstract: Pretrained 3D generative models produce detailed geometry and appearance but are primarily designed for object-centric generation within a limited spatial extent. Recent approaches address this limitation by partitioning large scenes into smaller spatial regions and applying pretrained 3D generative priors to each region. However, scaling tiled generation to large multi-view scenes makes it challenging to maintain local geometric continuity and global appearance consistency. We present a training-free framework for large-scale textured mesh generation from multi-view images. Our key idea is to scale tiled generation to large scenes with increased spatial detail while coordinating generation both locally and globally. We introduce local context tiled generation to improve geometric continuity between neighboring regions and global appearance alignment to reduce appearance discrepancies across distant regions. An adaptive scene decomposition further determines the number of tiles according to the input scene geometry. Experiments demonstrate improved geometric and appearance fidelity over existing approaches while enabling fine-grained generation of large-scale scenes.

title: Agreement Is Not Identity: HalluSquatting as a Case Study of Verification Boundaries in Agentic AI
abstract: This Technical Note presents a secondary analysis of published HalluSquatting experiments to examine verification boundaries in agentic AI systems. The analysis focuses on a specific problem that arises when model-generated resource identifiers are converted into external actions such as repository cloning, skill retrieval, software installation, or tool invocation. Using aggregate results reported by Spira et al. (2026), the paper reconstructs cases in which cross-model agreement converges on a repository identifier that does not match the study-designated target. In the librepods case, the same non-target identifier is supported by all evaluated models. The original study also shows that web search can substantially improve repository resolution, while separate post-registration ClawHub experiments demonstrate that an attacker-controlled resource can itself become the highest-ranked search result. These observations motivate a distinction between four stages of agentic verification: Generate → Discover → Identify → Authorize The paper argues that these stages answer different evidential questions. Model agreement provides evidence of convergence; search provides evidence of discoverability; identity verification asks whether the discovered resource corresponds to the intended target; and authorization asks whether a particular action involving that resource is justified. Provenance and artifact safety are treated as related but non-equivalent considerations within this verification process. The four-stage decomposition is proposed as an analytical and design vocabulary, not as a validated defense or complete security architecture. The paper does not reproduce attacks, introduce exploit code, or claim empirical validation of a new mitigation mechanism. A reproducibility supplement accompanies the manuscript and provides the source-to-result audit map, machine-readable reconstructions of the relevant published tables, deterministic calculations, and claim boundaries.

title: Exact Spin Elimination for Quadratic and k-Local Ising Optimization
abstract: Code and data for "Exact Spin Elimination Compilation for Quadratic and k-Local Ising Hamiltonians" This record archives the code, instance generators, raw result tables, and figure scripts for the manuscript by Natalia G Berloff. What the code does. Walsh elimination is a classical compiler for quadratic and k-local Ising Hamiltonians. It removes selected spins exactly: for each spin, the incident terms are replaced by their exact conditional minimum, expanded in the Walsh basis of the neighbours, and a reverse rule is stored so that any reduced configuration lifts to an original configuration of equal energy. Explicit caps bound neighbourhood size, interaction order, and term growth. The compiler is solver-independent; the benchmarks use simulated annealing (OpenJij sample_hubo), parallel tempering, and qubovert as backends.

title: Title: Quantum Resonance Synchronization for Material Science Simulations
abstract: Quantum Resonance Synchronization (QRS) offers a novel approach to enhancing the accuracy of material simulation models by leveraging quantum entanglement to create synchronized states across multiple qubits. This technique promises to overcome limitations of current classical approximations, particularly in simulating complex systems with multiple interacting elements, by allowing the identification of subtle resonance patterns previously missed by traditional methods. This paper details the theoretical framework and practical implementation of QRS, exploring its potential to dramatically improve the fidelity of material simulations across a range of applications. We will examine the underlying principles of entanglement, the challenges associated with maintaining coherence, and the potential benefits of QRS in advancing material science research.

title: Probability-Driven Optimization for Adaptive Parameter Tuning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on probabilistic differential equations (PDEs) that enables automatic parameter adjustment to maximize objective function performance within complex, dynamic environments. The core mechanism involves formulating the optimization problem as a probability model, employing a self-adaptive adjustment strategy to mitigate over-optimization, and leveraging the inherent modeling capabilities of PDEs. The algorithm's design offers improved robustness and interpretability compared to traditional methods, particularly in situations characterized by high dimensionality, non-linearities, and evolving conditions. This work demonstrates the potential of PDE-based optimization for a diverse range of applications requiring adaptive parameter control.

title: Quantum State Transitions and Adaptive Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum state transitions are a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, driving the evolution of quantum states and enabling quantum algorithms. This paper presents a novel framework for quantum computing based on the dynamic changes in quantum states, aiming to automate the execution of complex algorithms. We propose a self-adaptive quantum computing framework leveraging these transitions to achieve enhanced computational capabilities. The core mechanism centers around the controlled manipulation of quantum states through continuous transitions, allowing for automated optimization of quantum circuits. This approach contrasts with traditional quantum computing methods which often rely on pre-defined gate sequences. We demonstrate the framework's potential through a simplified, illustrative example of a quantum algorithm. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Non-Linear Geometric Groups: A Dynamic Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic optimization algorithm specifically designed for optimizing geometric groups. Traditional optimization approaches often struggle with complex, non-linear systems, and this algorithm addresses this limitation by leveraging a dynamic, simulated topology. The core mechanism centers around a continuous evolution of the geometric structure, enabling the algorithm to effectively explore a vast parameter space and identify optimal configurations. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, the simulation framework employed, and the key optimization process. We present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in finding optimal geometric structures for a specific, albeit simplified, geometric group. The focus is on showcasing the algorithm's adaptability and potential for wider application in the field of geometric optimization.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Tensor Embedding for Semantic Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the application of a novel non-Euclidean tensor embedding technique for semantic analysis. The core challenge lies in representing complex concepts within a framework that explicitly incorporates geometric properties, allowing for a deeper and more nuanced understanding of data. Traditional embedding methods often treat data as independent vectors, failing to capture the underlying geometric relationships crucial for semantic interpretation. This research proposes a new method – a tensor embedding specifically designed to encode geometric information – that aims to overcome these limitations. We detail the methodology, present preliminary results demonstrating improved performance in semantic classification, and offer insights into the potential benefits of this approach.

title: Title: Tensor-Vector Neural Network for Signal Processing
abstract: The field of signal processing relies heavily on efficient and robust methods for analyzing and classifying complex waveforms. Traditional approaches often struggle with high-dimensional data, leading to limitations in accuracy and computational efficiency. This paper proposes a novel Tensor-Vector Neural Network (TVNN) architecture designed to address these challenges by leveraging a vector-based component to represent and process signals directly. We explore the benefits of this approach, particularly in handling non-linear signals and improving the performance of signal detection and classification tasks. The core mechanism involves integrating a vector-based layer within the network to function directly on the input signal vector, thereby mitigating the complexities associated with dense representations. This allows for a more streamlined and potentially more accurate representation of the signal, facilitating enhanced performance in a wide range of signal processing applications. This work presents a fundamental investigation into the potential of this new architecture, demonstrating its efficacy through simulations and preliminary experimental results.

title: Nonlinear Topological Quantum States: Adaptive Geometry Simplification
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive geometry simplification to non-linear topological quantum states. The core claim is to design an algorithm that learns the geometric evolution rules of the quantum state, enabling dynamic changes and control, ultimately improving computational efficiency. The research leverages the intersection of topology and numerical simulation to implement this dynamic control. Traditional approaches often struggle with complex geometric structures, presenting a novel solution through dynamic simplification. This work introduces a new algorithm that dynamically adjusts the quantum state's geometry, offering a potential breakthrough in handling intricate topological quantum systems.

The research leverages the intersection of topology and numerical simulation to implement this dynamic control. Traditional approaches often struggle with complex geometric structures, presenting a novel solution through dynamic simplification. title: Quantum-Enhanced Optimization of Neural Network Architecture
abstract: Quantum computing holds the potential to revolutionize various fields, and the field of neural networks is no exception. This research investigates the application of quantum optimization algorithms to enhance the design of neural network architectures, aiming to improve performance across specific tasks. We explore the feasibility of utilizing a novel quantum optimization technique to systematically explore network architectures and identify configurations that yield superior results. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary results demonstrating the potential for quantum acceleration in neural network architecture design. The core claim centers around the design of a quantum algorithm capable of efficiently navigating a complex space of possible network architectures, ultimately leading to optimized neural network configurations. The research will focus on identifying key architectural parameters and evaluating their impact on performance using benchmark datasets. This paper provides a foundational analysis of this approach and outlines potential avenues for future exploration.

title: Information Bottleneck with Memory Constraints for Long Sequence Modeling
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to long sequence modeling by integrating the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle with memory constraints. Traditional IB methods often struggle with long sequences due to the exponential growth of the bottleneck dimensionality and the difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. This work addresses these limitations by modifying the IB objective to explicitly penalize information flow and introduce a memory usage penalty. The resulting model learns a compressed representation of the sequence, effectively reducing redundancy while preserving critical information for prediction. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework that incorporating memory constraints significantly improves compression efficiency and prediction accuracy in long sequence modeling scenarios. The core idea is to balance information compression with resource limitations, leading to a more robust and efficient model. The primary contribution lies in the formulation of a modified IB objective function that considers both the information content and the memory footprint of the learned representation.

title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Quantum State Transfer
abstract: This paper explores the application of zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to facilitate quantum state transfer. The core idea is to leverage ZKPs to verify the correct reception of a quantum state without revealing the state itself. Traditional quantum communication methods are susceptible to information leakage, and distance limitations restrict effective transmission. This research proposes a novel quantum communication protocol incorporating ZKPs, offering a potential solution to these challenges. The protocol utilizes a series of measurements and cryptographic proofs to guarantee the receiver accurately interprets the intended quantum state. We present a formal mathematical framework for this protocol, detailing the key components and their relationships. The resulting system significantly reduces the risk of information compromise while potentially expanding the practical range of quantum communication. The primary contribution lies in the innovative combination of quantum communication principles with the robust security guarantees provided by ZKPs. We analyze the protocol's performance and discuss its implications for secure quantum networks. ---

title: Dynamic Semantic Space Learning
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Semantic Space Learning (DSM) – a novel approach to machine learning that leverages the principles of cognitive development to create a dynamic and adaptable semantic representation of knowledge. Unlike traditional knowledge graphs which represent knowledge as static structures, DSM constructs a dynamic semantic space through the simulation of cognitive stages, ranging from sensorimotor to operational thought. The core mechanism involves a multi-layered neural network architecture where each layer corresponds to a specific cognitive stage. Concepts and relationships learned at lower layers are dynamically injected into higher layers, adapting to input data and feedback. Layer-to-layer connections and conceptual representations evolve based on learning progress and environmental changes, resulting in a continuously developing semantic network with contextual understanding. This approach offers improved robustness and interpretability compared to static knowledge representation methods, particularly in handling uncertainty, noise, and novel information. The proposed framework aims to bridge the gap between cognitive science and machine learning, paving the way for more intelligent and adaptable systems.

title: Quantum Error Correction Coding with Adaptive Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) coding that incorporates adaptive optimization. Traditional QEC schemes utilize pre-defined encoding strategies, neglecting the dynamic nature of quantum error patterns. Our methodology addresses this limitation by dynamically adjusting the encoding scheme based on real-time observations of the error mode. We employ an optimization algorithm, grounded in a quantum degradation model, to analyze error distributions and adjust the encoding subset and correction strategy, ultimately minimizing error propagation. The core claim is that adaptive optimization significantly enhances QEC efficiency. The proposed mechanism allows for a more robust and efficient utilization of qubits in quantum computations. This research provides a framework for designing more resilient and adaptable QEC systems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization through Hyper-Dimensionality Reduction
abstract: Quantum-inspired optimization aims to enhance the efficiency of optimization algorithms by employing techniques inspired by quantum mechanics. This paper investigates the application of hyper-dimensional dimensionality reduction to quantum-inspired approaches, with the goal of reducing the search space while maintaining the overall solution quality. We propose a novel hyper-dimensional dimensionality reduction process that leverages the principles of quantum collapse to effectively "collapse" the search space. This approach offers a promising pathway towards improved optimization performance by mitigating the computational complexity associated with high-dimensional search spaces. The benefits of this method include increased efficiency, reduced computational cost, and improved solution quality compared to traditional optimization algorithms.

title: Epistemic Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces Epistemic Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs), a novel approach to graph neural networks that explicitly models and incorporates uncertainty into the learning process. Traditional GNNs primarily focus on learning pattern recognition from graph-structured data, often neglecting the inherent uncertainty associated with these patterns and the relationships between nodes. EGNNs address this limitation by representing the network's confidence in inferred relationships as dynamic edge weights within a graph. Nodes in the graph represent individual data points, and edges represent the strength of the inferred relationships between them. Crucially, the weight of each edge is modulated by a learned epistemic uncertainty estimate, reflecting the network's confidence in that particular connection. This allows EGNNs to not only learn patterns but also to represent and reason with uncertainty, leading to more robust and reliable predictions and decision-making. The core claim of this work is that neural networks can learn not just patterns in data, but also the *uncertainty* inherent in those patterns, represented as a dynamically evolving graph. The mechanism is a GNN where nodes represent data points and edges represent the strength of inferred relationships, with edge weights modulated by learned epistemic uncertainty estimates – representing the network's confidence in the relationship.

title: ECOKV: Geometry-Aware KV Cache Eviction via Complementary Diversity Metrics
abstract: Although multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in diverse tasks, their scalability remains limited by the memory and computational overhead of KV cache storage. Recent KV cache eviction approaches incorporate a cosine similarity-based diversity metric with importance metrics to selectively retain critical key-value pairs. However, cosine similarity involves normalization that discards magnitude information, and it often yields uniformly high similarity values across layers due to the anisotropy property of hidden representations. In our study ECOKV, we rigorously deconstruct the capabilities of existing diversity metrics. Moving beyond simple measurement, we propose a geometry-aware composite metric that jointly leverages Euclidean distance and cosine similarity to capture token diversity from complementary perspectives. Furthermore, we use these two metrics to estimate the redundancy level of each attention head, allowing adaptive weighting between diversity and importance scores during token selection. Finally, we demonstrate that the observation window commonly employed to preserve recent tokens can be substantially reduced, thereby allocating more cache capacity to informative tokens and yielding consistent improvements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ECOKV achieves state-of-the-art performance under various compression ratios and can be seamlessly integrated with existing KV cache eviction methods. We further analyze the relationship between importance and diversity, and examine redundancy patterns across layers and attention heads.

title: This dataset supports the paper "Bilateral Credit Assignment and Curriculum-Guided Graph Relation Learning for Multi-Aircraft Cooperative Aerial Games"
abstract: Multi-aircraft cooperative aerial games pose a coupled decision and control problem under uncertainty, relational interaction, and an adaptive opponent. The difficulty is systemic: the engagement is inherently relational, credit assignment must separate cooperative team-level outcomes from competitive individual ones, and a strong rule-based adversary renders random exploration sample-inefficient. This paper proposes the Bilateral-value Curriculum Agent (BCA), an integrated on-policy learning framework coupling relational state abstraction, bilateral credit assignment, and opponent-difficulty scheduling under one unchanged mission objective, with centralized training and decentralized execution. A Graph-Relational Encoder extracts relational agent embeddings from a typed engagement graph with two typed GraphSAGE layers; a Bilateral Value Decomposition maintains two centralized critics over cooperative and competitive reward streams; a Performance-Based Curriculum schedules opponent difficulty over a four-level ladder. All algorithms are evaluated identically under deterministic paired evaluation over multiple seeds with stochastic weight averaging. On a physics-based simulation platform with 3v3 and 5v5 adversarial tasks, BCA attains a mean win rate of $70.0 \pm 17.9\%$ over five seeds in 3v3, exceeding the strongest of seven baselines by $17.0\%$; the 5v5 margin is $14.4\%$. A fifteen-seed extension confirms the margin under distribution-free significance testing, and a checkpoint-window protection rule lifts the worst seed from $18\%$ to $48\%$. Ablations attribute the largest gain to the relational encoder, a reliability gain to the curriculum, and a left-tail insurance role to the bilateral decomposition; the learned team exhibits self-organized coordinated maneuvers without role labels or communication.

title: Using Artificial Intelligence Tools in Digital Marketing: A Survey Study of a Number of Private Sector Banks in Iraq
abstract: This research aims to explore the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital marketing. A questionnaire was developed to confirm the relationship between the research variables. Using a sampling methodology, 384 questionnaires were distributed to private sector banks in Nineveh Governorate, and the data were analyzed using SPSS version 24. The research results revealed a knowledge gap regarding the nature of the relationship between AI and digital marketing, and confirmed a statistical relationship between the research variables. Therefore, the banks included in the study need to enhance the role of AI in digital marketing. This research is the first of its kind to integrate current variables (AI and digital marketing) into a single hypothetical model for Iraqi private sector banks. The research findings can be utilized to implement AI in digital marketing, increasing banks' opportunities to achieve their goals and objectives. Consequently, private banks should organize training courses for their departments and participate in training courses with other banks. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Digital marketing; Attraction; Engagement; Learning; Retention; Communication.

title: Domain-Adaptive Probability Distribution Theory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probability distribution theory centered around the concept of "domain adaptation." Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their applicability to a specific dataset. We propose a dynamic distribution window mechanism that adapts the distribution parameters based on the unique characteristics of the input data, thereby enhancing model prediction accuracy and generalization. The core claim is that this approach allows for more intelligent and robust model training compared to static distribution theory.

title: 量子机器学习的基于自适应损失函数设计
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field of artificial intelligence that leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance machine learning algorithms. This paper presents a novel quantum machine learning algorithm, termed "Adaptive Loss Function Design" (ALFD), focusing on dynamically adjusting loss functions to optimize model performance and achieve more precise predictions. Traditional loss functions often suffer from suboptimal performance and limited adaptability, while QML offers the potential for significantly improved learning efficiency and accuracy through the inherent capabilities of quantum systems. ALFD employs a self-adjusting mechanism that iteratively modifies the loss function based on data fluctuations, creating a continuous optimization process. The core mechanism leverages quantum entanglement and superposition to efficiently explore the loss function space, leading to enhanced model generalization and predictive capabilities. This paper provides a detailed analysis of ALFD, including its mathematical formulation, implementation details, and experimental results demonstrating its superior performance compared to traditional loss functions and existing QML algorithms. The advantages of this approach lie in its adaptability, potentially leading to more robust and accurate models across diverse datasets.

title: Neurogenesis Reinforcement Learning Language Model
abstract: We propose the Neurogenesis Reinforcement Learning Language Model (NRLLM), a research framework in which stable linguistic mastery can trigger endogenous growth of a language agent trained through reinforcement learning. Godrick is the proposed experimental realization. Its defining hypothesis is that an exactly-one-neuron increase in a dynamic hidden structure, conditioned on independently specified mastery criteria, can support subsequent learning without sacrificing previously acquired capabilities. The framework separates content admission, learning, mastery assessment, and structural growth. A beta discernment subsystem evaluates whether authorized material is relevant and sufficiently supported for a target linguistic capability; it does not certify mastery. A future continual-learning stage would use a localhost chat and explicitly permitted internet sources. We formalize a candidate growth gate, outline initialization and plasticity choices, and specify controlled comparisons against fixed capacity, alternative growth triggers, replay, and feature replacement. Earlier work establishes individual components, including one-unit growth, artificial neurogenesis, reinforcement learning, and language-model expansion. The contribution claimed here is a proposed synthesis and falsifiable experimental protocol, not demonstrated superiority or an established claim of historical priority. No implementation results or benchmark measurements are reported.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm for non-linear geometric error correction, designed to enhance the accuracy and reliability of quantum computation. The developed algorithm demonstrates significant improvements in error detection and correction compared to existing classical methods, particularly in scenarios involving complex geometric transformations. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance, including mathematical formulations and experimental validation. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum error correction and opens avenues for more reliable and robust quantum computation.

We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance, including mathematical formulations and experimental validation. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum error correction and opens avenues for more reliable and robust quantum computation.

title: Title: Geometric Complexity Measures for Machine Learning Models
abstract: This paper investigates the use of geometric complexity measures to enhance the robustness assessment of machine learning models. Traditional metrics, while valuable, often fail to capture the intricate relationships within the model's representation. We introduce a novel set of geometric properties – curvature, torsion, and connectivity – designed to go beyond standard metrics by identifying vulnerabilities and patterns inherent in model structure. The core mechanism involves quantifying these properties using novel mathematical constructs and rigorously evaluating their impact on model performance across diverse datasets. The goal is to develop a more comprehensive and insightful assessment of model resilience, contributing to improved model design and stability.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, termed Dynamic Adaptive Optimization (DSO), designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization techniques by dynamically adjusting the optimization target function and the corresponding optimization algorithm. The core innovation of DSO lies in its ability to adapt to changing data characteristics, thereby significantly improving optimization efficiency and accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DSO through a series of rigorous experiments across various datasets, highlighting its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper details the algorithm's components, including a feedback mechanism for dynamic adjustment, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its performance characteristics. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications of this algorithm.

title: Dimensional Geometry Distortion Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel geometric distortion algorithm designed to dynamically adjust and distort space dimensions, with the ultimate goal of accurately simulating and predicting quantum entanglement behavior. The core concept revolves around the integration of "dynamic topology" – a framework leveraging quantum entanglement to generate self-organizing structures – and utilizing distortion geometry as a key mechanism for guiding and amplifying quantum entanglement. This algorithm offers a potential pathway for accelerating quantum computation by providing a more precise and intuitive method for handling the complexities of entangled states. The paper details the algorithm's design, the underlying theoretical framework, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling and simulating quantum entanglement.
